newsitem.title: UK: Experts urge universal hepatitis vaccination.
newsitem.headline: Experts urge universal hepatitis vaccination.

text.p: Vaccinating the entire population against hepatitis is cheaper than treating victims of the virus, Belgian experts said on Friday.

In a report for the British Medical Journal, Pierre van Damme and a team from the University of Antwerp's Centre for the Evaluation of Vaccination urged governments which did not have universal vaccination to introduce it at once.
"Although safe and effective hepatitis B vaccines have been available for over 10 years, universal vaccination is still being postponed in many countries," they wrote.
"One reason is the weakness of our social commitment to preventive medicine and vaccines. Important also is the lack of medical and public awareness."
The hepatitis B virus, 100 times more infectious than the HIV virus that causes AIDS, can badly damage the liver. It is the second-biggest cause of cancer after smoking.
More than a third of the world's population have been infected, according to liver disease experts.
Some 80 countries, including the United States, Germany, France and Spain, have national vaccination plans for children, with at least 80 million people being vaccinated globally.
But Van Damme's group complained that many countries -- notably Britain -- did not vaccinate everyone.

"Some decision-makers in northern Europe are not convinced that the burden of disease of hepatitis B justifies the expense of universal vaccination," Van Damme wrote. But they said cost-effectiveness studies showed this was untrue.
British health officials argued against Van Damme's recommendations. British government policy is to support vaccination only for "at risk" groups.
"We...suggest that at present it would be preferable to concentrate on reinforcing existing strategies," Philip Mortimer and Elizabeth Miller of the Central Public Health Laboratory wrote in a reply.
But they also called current implementation of government policy "halfhearted" and unacceptable. Only a minority of pregnant women were screened for hepatitis.

Up to 90 percent of babies born to infected mothers become chronically infected with hepatitis, which kills 25 percent of the babies who get it. Screening mothers is therefore seen as a good way to prevent the spread of the disease.
Britain's Children's Liver Disease Foundation and the Patients' Association earlier this month called on Britain to introduce universal vaccination.
